Senator Curry, Representative Gere and members of the Joint Select Committee on Housing
and Economic Development, my name is Andy Cashman. I am the Founder of Resolve
Government Relations. We represent the Maine Association of REALTORS�, a professional trade association established in 1936 with over 6,500 members statewide. REALTORS�

The Maine Association of REALTORS� supports LD 413 because it would address the
concern we had with amended language that was added to PL 2023, c. 602 with no
discussion last session. The law required a seller of residential real estate to disclose
information regarding actual or alleged violations of shoreland zoning ordinances applicable
to the property. LD 413 would remove the word "alleged" from the statute and we strongly
support this proposal.
Our members work diligently to ensure their clients comply with the letter of the law but it is more challenging to do that when the law is unclear. Here, "alleged" is not a defined which creates ambiguity when advising clients as to what should be disclosed. For example, does a conversation over the fence with a neighbor who suggests there`s a violation meet the threshold for an "alleged" violation -- or does it require a formal complaint? As written now, PL 2023, c. 602 has no clear distinction. Requiring disclosures of "alleged" violations is an
unreasonable burden for property owners and will likely lead to confusion for prospective
buyers when the allegation may later be unfounded. In addition, it is inconsistent with all of
the other existing required property disclosure laws in Title 33.
In turn, we believe that LD 413 clarifies shoreland violations requirements and provides clarity
for all parties involved in the transaction as well as limits possible burden on the court system
to manage litigation of alleged violations brought forward by interested parties. lf filings are
less prevalent, then the fiscal impacts will be less as a result.

Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and the honorable members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Housing and Economic Development. My name is Jack Duchanne and I
proudly represent the people of Cornville, Madison and Norridgewock in the Maine
House of Representatives. I come before you today to present LD 413, An Act Regarding
Disclosure by Sellers of Residential Real Property of Notices of Shoreland Zoning Ordinance Violations.

This bill should really be titled An Act to Clarify PL 2023 Chapter 602. That is the intent and sole pulpose of this bill. In the 131$` Legislature, LD 2101, An Act to Strengthen
Shoreland Zoning Enforcement was passed. This simple, common-sense bill gives municipalities and the Land Use Planning Commission the ability to suspend or revoke shoreland zoning violators' permits, and place liens on properties that are in violation. Municipalities desperately need this tool to keep themselves solvent when fighting the
worst and most egregious shoreland zone violators. BUT. . ..

The final piece of the bill as passed speaks to the Shoreland Zoning disclosure required
by real estate professionals. That language was changed in Sec. 5. 33 MRSA �173, sub-
�7 is enacted to read:

7. Notice of violation. Detailed information on an actual or alleged violation of a shoreland zoning ordinance adopted pursuant to Title 38, chapter 3, subchapter 1, article 2-B, including those that were state-imposed. imposed on and applicable to the

The common sense of the rest. of law seems to fail in the language enacted in Sec. 5. 33
MRSA �173, sub-�7. Including the word "alleged" in the requirement for disclosure
puts a property owner in an untenable position where if a neighbor "alleges" that they have violated the shoreland zoning ordinance but that "violation" has not been proven or
even proven by the municipal authority, their due process rights may be violated by this
law.
Requiring disclosure of an alleged but not adjudicated violation is a violation of the due
process of every property owner who wants to sell their property. There are no "guard rails" in the law as to who alleges the violation, to whom the violation must be reported
and any remedies for said alleged violation. The due process right, established by the Fourteenth Amendment, guarantees that the government cannot take a person's basic rights to "life, liberty, or property, without due process of law." This due process right is designed to protect citizens from actions taken by state government, counties, towns, and cities. Maine law, regardless of intent or aim of the statute cannot violate that.
Consider this: Mr. Smith owns property on North Pond. Mr. Jones owns property next to Mr. Smith. Mr. Jones alleges that Mr. Smith cut trees in the shoreland zone that he was not permitted to cut. Mr. Jones does not notify the local code enforcement officer but rather just tells Mr. Smith that he has done wrong. Mr. Smith decides to sell the property but fails to disclose that Mr. Jones has alleged that he cut trees inappropriately. There is no citation from the municipality or adjudication of the case by the appropriate authority but Mr. Smith would have to disclose that Mr. Jones "alleged" that trees were cut inappropriately, with no proof. This violates Mr. Smith's due process protection afforded in the 14"` Amendment.
I have proposed an amendment courtesy of Maine Municipal Association to fix this
language issue in the law that I have provided to your clerk. It replaces the words "actual or alleged" with clear guidelines that should protect buyers from buying a property with a shoreland zoning problem but also doesn't violate the sellers' due process rights.

the extent that I am able.
Thank you.

of land in the municipality violates a shoreland zoning ordinance. This includes requiring the violation to be removed, abated or otherwise corrected. If a municipality cannot achieve compliance, they are authorized to prosecute "alleged" violations in District Court. Unless and until a District Couit issues a decision affirming or denying that certain actions constitute a violation, all violations identified by a municipality are "alleged" . Therefore, a property owner can be required to take substantive and costly actions to correct alleged violations. If a property
with such violations is sold, the new owner may be required to correct those alleged
violations.
Prospective buyers should know what encumbrances and liabilities come with property they are considering buying. Unfortunately, the Department regularly encounters people who have
purchased property without that information. Arguably any shoreland zoning violations
_
identified by a municipality are a matter of public record and prospective buyers could perform
their own due diligence by requesting municipal records. However, very few buyers seek
information beyond what is provided on the required disclosure forms, particularly for residential
properties.
LD 413 proposes to amend recently enacted residential real property disclosure requirements to
remove violations that are enforceable against current and future property owners. This will
unreasonably remove many legitimate enforcement cases from the scope of this disclosure
provision, greatly diminishing its value to purchasers of real estate. Property owners subject to notice of violations, negotiating administrative consent agreements, and even parties to District Court enforcement proceedings are all still "alleged violators" .
The Department can certainly understand the due process protections likely intended by this bill. Complaints or allegations that lack merit should not impair the selling of property. However, this bill goes well beyond that. Removing "alleged" removes all violations until the violations have
been fully adjudicated, despite how clear the facts on the ground might be. This demarcation
point is too late. Should the Committee wish to remove meritless claims, a better method might be to make more explicit that the header "Notice of Violation" defines the scope of what constitutes a "actual or alleged violation" and must be disclosed, perhaps by revising it to "Subject to a Notice of Violation" . In those cases, it's not just a disgruntled neighbor or a property dispute weaponizing government enforcement, it's a Code Enforcement officer or other position with authority to enforce the ordinance, pursuing a violation they have investigated and issued written notice of. It appears that is already the intent of the current language, which properly balances interests of the owner with the bona fide notice interests of a prospective buyer, and enhances the protections delivered by shoreland zoning.
Thank you for your time and the opportunity to speak today. I am happy to answer any
questions.

Testimony of the Maine Municipal Association
Neither For Nor Against
LD 413 - An Act Regarding Disclosure by Sellers of Residential Real Property of Notices of Shoreland Zoning Ordinance Violations
February 27, 2025
Sen. Curry, Rep. Gere and distinguished members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee, my name is Rebecca Graham, and I am submitting testimony in neither for nor against LD 413 at the direction of MMA's Legislative Policy Committee (LPC) based on proposed amendments to the bill following discussions with the sponsor.
As originally drafted, the bill removes the word "alleged" from statute meaning no disclosure of a pending action from the state, court, or local municipality would be disclosed to a buyer until the final court judgement has been in place and all appeals had been exhausted. After conversations with the sponsor of LD 413, the Association believes this is not the intent, but rather to solve the problem of vexations of neighborhood complaints that have not resulted in any enforcement action.
Shoreland zone violations follow the land, not the violator, meaning any pending litigation of a municipal notice of violation such as clearing a wide space of trees to improve a water view against shoreland zone rules which could increase the land's retail value but would be inherited by a new owner with no notice. This could cause considerable unexpected expenses to both the new owner and the municipality which would then be required to issue a notice of violation the new owner to remedy the situation, while the original violator profited.
The Association agrees the word "alleged" is quite broad, but also includes court decisions that have not yet been exhausted by appeal. For this reason, MMA recommends the following amendment language as a possible solution with consideration and approval from Rep. Ducharme:
8. Notice of violation. Detailed information on an actual or alleged any notice of violation issued by a code enforcement officer and any pending enforcement action, court judgment or consent agreement involving violation of a shoreland zoning ordinance adopted pursuant to Title 38, chapter 3, subchapter 1, article 2-B, including those that were state-imposed, imposed on and applicable to the property.
This language will cover the whole process from notice of violation to court judgement or consent agreement without requiring the disclosure of neighbor and informal complaints that have not been acted upon.
With regret, staff are unable to attend the public hearing today as we are holding our monthly Legislative Police Committee meeting but will attend a work session for this bill and able to answer any additional questions the committee may have at that time. Thank you for your consideration!
